Positive associations/effects were also reported for 'Time Weighted Metrics: General' (3/9; 33%), 'Time Weighted Exposure: Addiction' (2/7; 29%), 'Place Visits: Addiction' (2/7; 29%), 'Movement Patterns: Variability' (2/5; 40%) and 'Movement Patterns: Speed' (2/5; 40%), although none of these studies used experimental designs. None of the studies reporting an association between a GPS feature incorporating addiction-specific locations and outcomes found a negative association, though some study findings were coded as 'mixed' (e.g., tobacco outlet proximity was associated with increased smoking urges near home but not farther away).

In contrast, a few associations/effects between 'Movement Patterns: Speed' (2/5; 40%) and 'Movement Patterns: Distance' (4/16; 25%) and substance use were negative, all in studies focused on cannabis, opioids or polysubstance use (e.g., self-reported intoxication was associated with shorter distances travelled).

Acceptability of the GPS data collection itself was reported in only 14/57 (25%) studies, all of which judged it to be acceptable.

Twelve studies (12/57; 21%) delivered a GPS-triggered intervention: four used randomised controlled trial designs, three were uncontrolled pre-post evaluations and five were single-arm feasibility/acceptability studies (see Table 1). The most frequently reported decision-rules involved triggering an intervention message if the user entered/dwelled in a location in which they had previously reported the addictive behaviour of interest (6/12; 50%), entered/dwelled in a prespecified high-risk location (3/12; 25%) or was in the proximity of a pre-specified high-risk location (2/12; 17%). The decision-rule was unspecified in one study (1/12; 8%). Where reported, GPStriggered intervention messages focused on coping strategies, motivational enhancement or outcome expectancies. Most studies evaluating GPS-triggered interventions reported that participants found the intervention to be acceptable (11/12; 92%); the remaining study did not assess/report participant acceptability.

Reported barriers to GPS data collection (see Figure 4) included technical issues (e.g., battery depletion, device malfunction or loss, device compatibility and geofencing issues), missing data resulting from app inactivity and reduced GPS accuracy, particularly indoors. Device compatibility requirements sometimes led to participants with older smartphones being excluded from taking part, thus raising equity concerns. Participant burden was mainly associated with repetitive EMAs and intervention messaging, rather than passive GPS data collection.

Methodological practices and considerations

The methodological practices and considerations in the included studies are summarised in Table 3. Most studies used participants' own smartphone devices for GPS data collection (33/57; 58%), followed by study provided smartphones (18/57; 32%) or dedicated GPS loggers (5/57; 8.8%). Only 16/57 (28%) studies reported the brand/model of the GPS device; the most frequently reported device was the Qstarz BT-Q1000X/XT GPS logger (3/16; 19%). Of the studies reporting the GPS sampling frequency (36/57; 63%), the most common sampling frequency was ≤1 minute (16/36; 44%), followed by >5 minutes (7/36; 19%). Of the studies reporting the temporal aggregation used (20/57; 35%), the most commonly reported temporal units were <1 hour and 24 hours (each 7/20; 35%). Of the studies reporting the spatial aggregation (13/57; 23%), the most commonly reported spatial scale was multiple spatial scales (5/13; 38%) or 50-100m (4/13; 31%). Just under half of the included studies (28/57; 49%) linked the raw coordinates to points of interest (POI) or area-level contextual data (see Table 3 and the Supplementary Materials 3), most commonly from official licensing registries (11/57; 19%), followed by commercial business lists (6/57; 11%), area-level data (6/57; 11%) and participant-or researcher-defined locations (5/57; 8.8%); three studies (3/57; 5.3%) did not report the POI data source. Few studies reported verifying the accuracy of POI locations.

Few of the included studies reported the intended GPS wear time (11/57; 19%) or the proportion of missing GPS data in the analytical sample (7/57; 12%). Almost a quarter reported a cut-off for including participants in the analytical sample (13/57; 23%), most commonly excluding participants when all their GPS data were missing (6/13; 46%). Almost a third reported filtering out noise in the GPS data (17/57; 30%), most commonly through 'manual cleaning' (11/17; 65%), and a quarter reported how missing GPS data were managed (14/57; 25%). Table 4 maps these practices onto the 'best practice' themes proposed in Pearson et al. (2024).

Most of the included studies did not share data or code with other researchers in an open science repository (48/57; 84%). Few studies considered the Modifiable Areal Unit Problem or the Uncertain Geographic Context Problem (10/57; 18%) and fewer still conducted sensitivity analyses to examine the robustness of the results to the selected spatial scale (6/57; 11%).

The most frequently reported methodological trade-offs reflected a prioritisation of smartphonebased data collection over dedicated GPS loggers, driven by greater scalability, low participant burden and the ability to integrate GPS with other data types (particularly EMAs) within a single device (see Figure 5). These benefits were balanced against lower GPS fidelity than dedicated loggers, missing data arising from battery optimisation and operating system restrictions, and reduced ability to capture fine-grained movement patterns. Privacy considerations or data storage constraints were rarely discussed as factors influencing methodological choices.

Quality appraisal

Of the studies involving an observational component, two were rated as 'Good', with the remaining 43 studies rated as 'Poor', mainly due to two shortcomings. First, over half of the studies (24/45; 53%) did not adjust for key confounders, while a further six failed to report their methods clearly enough to determine if any adjustment had occurred (Q14). Second, almost half of the studies (19/45; 42%) failed to report their retention rates (Q13). None reported blinding of outcome assessors (Q12).

Of the four controlled studies, two were rated as 'Good', one as 'Fair', and one as 'Poor', with lower ratings largely driven by a lack of blinding of participants and outcome assessors. Of the three prepost studies, two were rated as 'Good' and one as 'Poor', with methodological weaknesses characteristic of early-stage feasibility research, including small sample sizes and recruitment methods susceptible to selection bias (see the Supplementary Materials 4).

DISCUSSION

Most of the included studies focused on tobacco/nicotine, alcohol or polysubstance use, with only a single study focusing on gambling. The findings demonstrate a substantial interest in individual-level spatial tracking but also highlight conceptual and methodological limitations that currently constrain the field's progress.

Theoretical rationale for GPS-derived features

The most frequently extracted GPS-derived features were proximity-based exposure metrics, including exposure to tobacco or alcohol retail outlets and to personalised high-risk locations, yet most studies provided little explicit theoretical justification for why these features were selected. This may partly reflect the nascent stage of the field (Chaix et al., 2012). For example, although person-specific cues explain variance in subsequent cravings beyond generic, substance-specific cues (Fatseas et al., 2015), identifying personally salient locations requires intensive participant onboarding and data processing, which may explain why these approaches remain relatively underused. Nevertheless, the predominance of proximity-based metrics aligns broadly with the availability hypothesis, whereby increased exposure to addictive commodities increases opportunities for use.

In addition, mobility patterns are shaped by social structures, routines and interpersonal relationships, yet the reviewed literature provided limited insight into why individuals are exposed to particular environments in the first place. Emerging work integrating GPS data with social network information may help address this gap by contextualising environmental exposure within broader social systems (Fancello et al., 2026).

Overall study results

Proximity-based exposure features were generally positively associated with addictive states and behaviours, and no studies reported clear negative associations, although several studies reported mixed or only moderated effects. Other features, such as measures of mobility variability and deviations from individual baselines, were examined less frequently but also showed some associations with addiction-related outcomes, suggesting that the stability, variability and periodicity of activity spaces may constitute important behavioural signals beyond simple exposure metrics (Perchoux et al., 2013).

A few studies focused on cannabis, opioids or polysubstance use reported negative associations between mobility-related features and substance use, consistent with reduced mobility during intoxication, which underscores the importance of avoiding overly generalised interpretations of GPS-derived features.

Notably absent from the literature were studies examining potentially protective exposures, such as green or blue spaces (Berry et al., 2021; Gascon et al., 2017), and few studies investigated broader environmental stressors such as neighbourhood crime or deprivation, although our search strategy was not specifically designed to capture such studies.

GPS data collection and GPS-triggered interventions appeared to be acceptable to participants, with burden mainly related to repeated EMA prompts and intervention messaging rather than passive GPS data collection itself. However, acceptability was assessed in only a minority of studies, highlighting the need for more consistent evaluation of participant experiences, including perceptions of burden, privacy and data security.

Methodological practices and considerations

Investigators frequently had to balance dedicated GPS devices, which typically provide higher spatial fidelity, against smartphones, which enable richer multimodal data collection but may compromise positional accuracy, with downstream implications for data quality and validity of results.

Most observational studies were rated as having poor methodological quality, primarily due to inadequate adjustment for confounding and poor reporting of participant retention. Failure to account for confounders such as socioeconomic position, urbanicity or baseline dependence severity can substantially bias estimates of environmental exposure effects, while the small samples and limited blinding of intervention studies reflect the feasibility-oriented nature of the current literature.

Strengths and limitations

To our knowledge, this is the first systematic review of individual-level GPS data in addiction research. Its strengths include its methodological breadth across observational, experimental and mixed methods designs and the mapping of methodological practices onto established spatial epidemiological best practices. Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, unlike previous reviews focusing exclusively on research-grade GPS devices (Pearson et al., 2024), we included studies using smartphones, which may introduce variability in positional accuracy but are often the most practical option for daily life research. Second, substantial heterogeneity in how GPS-derived features were defined, operationalised and aggregated precluded formal meta-analysis; for example, one included study demonstrated that different spatial definitions can meaningfully alter estimates of smoking event capture (Luken et al., 2023). Third, screening, data extraction, quality appraisal and coding were largely performed by a single reviewer (although all extracted data and quality ratings were double checked by the lead or senior author), which carries a higher risk of missed studies and extraction errors. Fourth, the search was restricted to English-language records and included records from publicly available scholarly publishing platforms, which may not have been peer reviewed.

Implications and avenues for future research

Drawing on the review findings, we propose a research agenda for advancing the use of GPS data in addiction science (see Table 5). Future research would benefit from theory-driven spatial feature extraction, where temporal resolution, spatial scale and analytical strategy are explicitly aligned with hypothesised behavioural mechanisms, and from transparent reporting of privacy-related methodological choices. Several identified gaps also warrant attention. The spatial dimension of gambling remains underexplored; although gambling is increasingly online, the role of physical environments and mobility remains poorly understood.

As GPS coordinates alone provide limited insight into what individuals are actually doing within environments, spatial data need to be integrated with EMA, physiological sensing and other types of behavioural data (Fancello et al., 2026) to clarify the meaning of mobility signals.

Finally, causal inference remained challenging. Individuals actively select and construct their daily activity spaces ('selective daily mobility') (Chaix et al., 2013), making it difficult to determine whether environmental exposures influence addictive behaviours or whether individuals selectively seek out such environments, and associations with outlet proximity are entangled with urbanicity, socioeconomic position, commuting patterns and social routines. Future studies should therefore use stronger causal designs, within-person analyses with clear temporal ordering and rigorous control for spatial and social confounding.

CONCLUSION

Individual-level GPS data are increasingly used to study addictive behaviours. Exposure to addictionrelevant locations tends to be positively associated with addiction-related states and behaviours. However, the evidence base is limited by weak theoretical grounding and inconsistent methodological practices and reporting, including inadequate control for confounding. ) 0 (0%) Sample Size (Analytical) 33.0 (16.0, 92.0) 38.0 (18.0, 92.0) 209.0 (108.5, 261.5) 28.0 (13.0, 48.0) 10.0 (4.0, 19.0) 63.5 (28.0, 160.0) 31.5 (14.0, 57.0) 25.0 (7.0, 92.0) Study Duration (Days) 29.0 (14.0, 42.0) 14.0 (14.0, 30.0) 196.0 (120.5, 280.5) 42.0 (31.0, 42.0) 28.0 (10.5, 218.5) 36.0 (28.0, 98.0) 30.0 (14.0, 98.5) 14.0 (14.0, 34.5) Not Reported 3 2 0 0 1 0 2 1 Study-Level Mean Age 37.0 (22.4, 41.5) 30.9 (21.0, 44.7) 39.5 (32.2, 41.0) 33.8 (33.6, 33.9) 37.7 (37.0, 39.0) 27.8 (22.4, 33.9) 30.6 (19.6, 41.2) 41.1 (30.9, 46.9) Not Reported 22 19 0 1 2 5 8 9 Female (%) 50.0 (40.0, 58.4) 50.0 (40.0, 59.6) 47.5 (38.3, 56.0) 46.7 (46.4, 47.0) 54.7 (25.0, 69.7) 49.5 (42.7, 58.9) 46.5 (25.0, 57.8) 55.3 (43.7, 59.6) Relapse Prevention Theory: potentially aligns with the theory, if such environments act as high-risk contexts.

Combine passive GPS data with EMA measures of craving, affect, social context and discrete substance use/gambling events; integrate wearable physiological sensing (e.g., heart rate, electrodermal activity), accelerometry and other passive smartphone data (e.g., Bluetoothbased social proximity); use semantic place annotation to characterise the activities occurring at visited locations. 9) Use designs that address selective daily mobility Individuals actively select and construct their daily activity spaces ('selective daily mobility'; see, for example, Chaix et al., 2013), making it difficult to determine whether environmental exposures influence addictive behaviours or vice versa. Most studies were observational, with few randomised designs.

Use within-person analyses that establish temporal ordering between exposure and outcome within theoretically informed time windows; examine the reverse direction (e.g., whether cravings precede outlet visits); exploit natural experiments (e.g., outlet openings/closures, changes in licensing or opening hours); use micro-randomised trials to estimate the proximal causal effects of GPS-triggered support and to optimise decision rules. 10) Assess and report acceptability, burden and privacy systematically Acceptability of GPS data collection was rarely assessed, and privacy and data storage were seldom discussed as factors shaping methodological choices. Device compatibility requirements sometimes excluded participants with older smartphones, raising equity concerns.

Assess acceptability using validated, theory-informed measures; report participant burden, withdrawal (and reasons for withdrawal), perceived privacy and trust; conduct qualitative work with under-represented groups, including people in treatment and those experiencing socioeconomic disadvantage; report privacy-preserving procedures (e.g., on-device processing, geomasking, secure storage); report device eligibility criteria and consider providing study devices to avoid excluding participants.
